title: The Mental Reset Button - Hit It
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart addresses the moment when a school year ends and a teacher moves straight from the last day into the list of projects saved up for the summer. He argues that professionals always have such a list, that the list never ends, and that this is exactly why a deliberate reset must come first. Borrowing the image of the reset button on an original Nintendo, he defines the Mental Reset Button as an event of at least twenty-four hours involving complete unproductivity and some final reflection on the year. His example is a colleague's decade-old tradition of an overnighter at a lake cabin on the last day of school, complete with food, fishing, a campfire and an awards ceremony with assigned nominations. The point of the ritual is that the constraints of time and place drop away and the shift from school-year pressure to summer decompression actually happens, so the drive home feels different from the drive up. He then turns on his younger self, who glorified work and felt he had no time to unplug, and tells readers not to repeat it. The closing instruction is to leave the professional-development books at home and go be a regular person for a while.
points: Stuart gives the reset a specification rather than a sentiment: at least twenty-four hours, no productivity at all, and some deliberate reflection on the year that just ended.
The argument that a professional's work is never done is used to justify rest rather than to excuse overwork, since a list that cannot be finished is a poor reason to skip recovery.
The lake-cabin overnighter works because distance and an overnight stay dissolve the usual constraints, which is what makes the mental shift from pressure to decompression stick.
The teacher awards, with categories assigned in advance and nominations written up, turn collegial encouragement into a repeatable annual ritual.
He names glorifying work as the trap of his own early career, when finishing with students immediately became preparation for next year's students.
quotes: We all make The List. This is because we are professionals, and a professional's work is never done.
But great professionals are great people leading great lives. That last word is important. So how do you plan to hit “Reset” on your professional brain before you tackle The List?
Too many great educators pretend that they can just power themselves through the last weeks of school and then plow straight into tackling The List. Don’t fool yourself; you need to reset.

Essentially, the overnighter is about doing everything but thinking about The List: we enjoy food, laughter, beer, and a campfire; we fish, we reminisce, we compete, we celebrate. Since we’re out in the middle of nowhere and staying the night, the constraints of time and space slip away as we mentally shift from the pressure of a school year into the decompression of summer break.

On the drive home the next morning, I always feel distinctly different than I did on the drive up. I’m excited for the summer, both its work and its relaxation. I’m thankful for the year that’s passed, free from any frustrations I was holding, and ready to start on The List in a more relaxed, refreshed fashion.
But some of you are like I was early on in my career — I glorified work. I felt like I had no time to reset or unplug.
